Search words: SI, metric, prefixes, dimensional analysis, significant figures, uncertainty, conversion.

children.note: A number without a unit says nothing: "the bridge is 40" could be metres or feet. Engineers in Kenya and nearly everywhere use SI, so a drawing from Nairobi reads the same in Mombasa or Mumbai.

children.topic: A quantity is defined by how it is measured
children.note: Length by a rule, time by a clock; speed is then calculated as distance over time. Define it by the method of measuring or by the formula from other measurements.

manas.q: How is a physical quantity defined?

children.topic: Two systems: SI and English units
children.note: SI (metric) is used by almost every country and by all of science. English (imperial) units — feet, pounds, miles — survive mainly in the USA. You will meet inch-based bolts ("SAE") on imported machines.

children.topic: SI is coordinated by the BIPM in Paris
children.note: The International Bureau of Weights and Measures keeps the definitions; since 2019 every base unit is fixed by a constant of nature, not by a metal object.

manas.q: Since 2019, what are SI base units defined by?

children.note: Everything measurable is built from seven base quantities. Learn the unit and its symbol: m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd. Symbols are case-sensitive: "K" is kelvin, "k" is kilo.

manas.q: Name the seven SI base units with their symbols.

children.note: Since 1983: how far light goes through empty space in 1/299 792 458 s. That fixes the speed of light at exactly 299 792 458 m/s — the constant defines the unit.

manas.q: How is the metre defined, and what number does that fix exactly?

children.note: Until 2019 a platinum–iridium cylinder near Paris, which slowly lost about 50 micrograms. Now fixed through the Planck constant and measured on a Kibble balance. The only base unit whose name carries a prefix.

manas.q: What replaced the metal cylinder as the definition of the kilogram?

children.note: Since 1967: the time for 9 192 631 770 vibrations of a caesium atom. GPS and M-Pesa timestamps depend on clocks this exact.

manas.q: What does the second count?

children.note: The base unit for electricity; charge (coulomb) is current × time, so 1 C = 1 A·s.
Thermodynamic temperature; 0 K is absolute zero. A kelvin step equals a Celsius step, and 0 °C = 273.15 K. Write "K", never "°K".

manas.q: Convert 25 °C to kelvin.

children.note: Counts particles (about 6.022 × 10²³ of them). Chemistry and materials courses use it constantly.
Brightness as the eye sees it; used in lighting design. Rare in first-year mechanics.
Multiply or divide base units and you get every other unit. 22 derived units have special names (newton, pascal, joule, watt…); each can still be written in base units.

manas.q: What is a derived unit? Give two examples.

children.note: Length × length and length × length × length. 1 litre is 10⁻³ m³ (a 10 cm cube), one of the non-SI units accepted with SI.

manas.q: How many cubic metres is one litre?

children.note: Distance over time, and change of speed over time. A car at 60 km/h is moving at about 16.7 m/s.
Mass per volume. Water is about 1000 kg/m³, the same as 1 g/cm³: 1000 kg = 10⁶ g spread over 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³. Steel is about 7850 kg/m³.

manas.q: What is the density of water in kg/m³?

children.note: From F = ma: one newton accelerates one kilogram at one metre per second squared. A 1 kg bag of sugar weighs about 9.8 N on Earth.

manas.q: Write the newton in base units.

children.note: Force spread over an area. Atmospheric pressure is about 101 kPa; a car tyre about 220 kPa above that.
Work = force × distance. Lifting that 1 kg bag by 1 m takes about 9.8 J. 1 kWh of electricity is 3.6 MJ.

manas.q: How many joules in one kilowatt-hour?

children.note: Energy per second. A 2 kW kettle uses 2000 J every second; a 100 W solar panel at full sun gives 100 J each second.
Angle = arc length ÷ radius, so metres cancel. Trig functions in physics formulas expect radians.
Degrees Celsius, litres and electron-volts are allowed but always convertible: °C = K − 273.15, 1 L = 10⁻³ m³, 1 t (tonne) = 1000 kg = 1 Mg.
One unit covers every scale by adding a power-of-ten prefix: nanometres in a chip, kilometres on a road. Memorise the common ones; the full table is on the OpenStax page.

manas.q: What do kilo, mega, giga, milli, micro and nano mean as powers of ten?

children.note: kilo, mega, giga, tera. A 5 GW power station; a 2 TB disk. Capital letters from mega upward.
milli, micro, nano, pico. A 3 mm bolt; a 10 µF capacitor; a 500 nm wavelength.
centi, deci, hecto, deka — common in everyday life (cm, dL, hectare = 100 m × 100 m) but engineers prefer steps of 1000.
No "megagigametre". For mass the prefix goes on the gram, not the kilogram: 1000 kg is 1 Mg (one megagram), also called a tonne.

manas.q: What is 1000 kg written with a single prefix?

children.note: Step 1: kg → g by × 10³, giving 1.93 × 10¹⁶ g. Step 2: the nearest prefixes are peta (10¹⁵) and exa (10¹⁸). Step 3: 10¹⁶ = 10 × 10¹⁵, so 19.3 Pg (petagrams) — a number between 1 and 1000.

manas.q: Express 1.93 × 10¹³ kg using one prefix so the number is between 1 and 1000.

children.note: Also correct, but the convention is a number between 1 and 1000 so the value reads naturally. Both are the same mass.

Multiply by a conversion factor — a fraction equal to one, such as (1 km / 1000 m) — arranged so the unwanted unit cancels. Write the units in every line; if they do not cancel, the fraction is upside down.

manas.q: What is a conversion factor and how do you know which way up to write it?

children.note: Multiply by (1 km per 1000 m): the metres cancel and 80 m becomes 0.080 km. Same answer by prefix: 8.0 × 10¹ m with kilo = 10³ gives 8.0 × 10⁻² km.
60 km/h × (1000 m / 1 km) × (1 h / 3600 s) = 16.7 m/s. Quick rule: divide km/h by 3.6.

manas.q: Convert 90 km/h to m/s.

children.topic: Worked: 10 miles in 20 minutes, in m/s
children.note: First in the given units: half a mile per minute. Then two factors — 1609 m per mile and one minute per 60 s — give 13 m/s. Two factors, two cancellations.
5 L × (10⁻³ m³ / 1 L) = 5 × 10⁻³ m³ = 0.005 m³. Mass of that water ≈ 1000 kg/m³ × 0.005 m³ = 5 kg.

manas.q: A 20-litre jerrycan of water: volume in m³ and mass in kg?

children.topic: Squared and cubed units need the factor twice or thrice
children.note: 1 m² = (100 cm)² = 10 000 cm²; 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³. Forgetting the power is the classic error in area and volume conversions.

manas.q: How many cm³ in 1 m³?

children.note: A walking speed of 1.4 m/s or a car at 25 m/s is believable; 1400 m/s is not. If the size is wrong by a thousand, a prefix was probably missed.

Every quantity has a dimension built from L (length), M (mass), T (time), I (current), Θ (temperature), N (amount) and J (light). Square brackets mean "dimension of": [v] = LT⁻¹. Dimensions obey algebra like units.

manas.q: What are the seven dimension symbols?

children.note: You can only add, subtract or equate quantities with the same dimension — no apples plus oranges. Both sides of an equation must agree.

manas.q: State the two rules of dimensional consistency.

children.topic: Rule 2: sin, cos, log, exp take pure numbers
children.note: Their arguments must be dimensionless, and their outputs are dimensionless too. sin(at²/s) is fine because LT⁻²·T²/L = 1.
All seven powers zero — a pure number. Angles in radians, ratios, π, 2, efficiency, strain.

children.topic: Worked: πr² or 2πr for the area of a circle?
children.note: [πr²] = 1·L² = L², the dimension of area. [2πr] = L, a length — so it is the circumference. Dimensions pick the right form but not the constant (they cannot tell πr² from 2πr²).

manas.q: Use dimensions to decide which of 4πr² and 4πr³/3 is the volume of a sphere.

children.topic: Worked: is s = vt + ½at² consistent?
children.note: [s] = L. [vt] = LT⁻¹·T = L. [½at²] = LT⁻²·T² = L. All three terms are lengths, so yes. Swap to s = vt² + ½at and the terms become LT and LT⁻¹ — nonsense.

manas.q: Check s = vt² + ½at for dimensional consistency.

children.topic: Uses: catch typos, rebuild forgotten formulas
children.note: A quick dimension check finds algebra slips before the calculator does. It also suggests how a new quantity must depend on others — a tool you will use in fluids (Reynolds number).
Dimensional analysis never finds a dimensionless factor such as ½ or 2π. Those come from the physics.
Measurements are never exact. Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is how closely repeats agree. A reported number should show only the digits you actually know.

manas.q: Explain the difference between accuracy and precision.

children.topic: Accurate vs precise: the GPS target picture
children.note: Dots spread wide but centred on the target: accurate, not precise. Dots tightly grouped but off-centre: precise, not accurate. A good instrument is both.
A length 2.00 m ± 0.02 m means the true value probably lies between 1.98 and 2.02 m. Percent uncertainty = δA/A × 100 % = 1 %.

manas.q: A mass is 5.0 kg ± 0.1 kg. What is the percent uncertainty?

children.topic: Multiplying or dividing: add percent uncertainties
children.note: Area of a 2.00 m ± 1 % by 1.50 m ± 2 % panel: 3.00 m² ± 3 %, i.e. ± 0.09 m².

children.topic: Significant figures: the digits you trust
children.note: 36.7 cm has three; 0.0025 m has two (leading zeros do not count); 1200 is ambiguous — write 1.2 × 10³ or 1.200 × 10³ to say what you mean.

manas.q: How many significant figures in 0.0025 and in 36.70?

children.topic: Multiplication and division: fewest sig figs wins
children.note: 2.3 m × 1.457 m = 3.4 m² (two figures, because 2.3 has only two).

children.topic: Addition and subtraction: fewest decimal places wins
children.note: 12.4 m + 0.057 m = 12.5 m (one decimal place, set by 12.4).

manas.q: 12.4 + 0.057 to the correct number of figures?

children.note: 9.8 m/s² × 5.0 kg = 49 N, not 49.000. Extra digits claim a precision you never measured.
The gap between your result and the accepted value. If it is bigger than your uncertainty, look for a systematic error (a mis-zeroed scale, a stretched tape).
Engineers estimate before they calculate — to size a pump, a budget, a tank — then check the detailed answer against the estimate. Aim for the right power of ten, not the last digit.

children.topic: Method: break it into things you know
children.note: Water for a 50-house estate: 50 houses × 5 people × 100 L/day ≈ 25 000 L/day = 25 m³/day. Each factor is a rough guess; the product is usually within a factor of 2–3.

manas.q: Estimate the daily water need of a 50-house estate and state your assumptions.

children.note: Write the answer as 10ⁿ: 25 m³ is "of order 10 m³". Two estimates that differ by a factor of 3 are the same order of magnitude.

children.topic: Check limits and units at the end
children.note: Does the estimate have the right unit? Does it grow the right way when one input grows? A per-day figure that is far above a river's flow is a sign something is wrong.
The errors first-years make most often — each one has cost marks or, in practice, money.

children.topic: Mixing km/h with m/s in one formula
children.note: Convert everything to base SI before you substitute. v = 60 into s = vt with t in seconds gives nonsense.

children.topic: Forgetting to square the factor for areas
children.note: 1 m² is 10 000 cm², not 100. Why: a square 1 m on each side is 100 cm by 100 cm, and area multiplies both sides, so the factor 100 is used twice. Check: picture a 1 km² plot as 1000 m × 1000 m = 10⁶ m².
The kilogram already has a prefix; 1000 kg is 1 Mg or 1 t.

children.topic: Degrees in a trig function expecting radians
children.note: Formulas such as ω = θ/t or arc = rθ need radians. Set the calculator mode before you start.
Round to the significant figures the data allow; keep extra digits only in the middle of a calculation.

children.topic: Writing units in the wrong case
children.note: kg not KG, m not M (M is mega), s not S (S is siemens), K not °K. The symbol is the unit's identity.
Say the answer aloud, then tap the bubble to check against the source page. Five questions, no calculator needed for most.

children.topic: Q1 · Write the pascal and the joule in base units
children.note: Pa = N/m² = kg·m⁻¹·s⁻². J = N·m = kg·m²·s⁻².

manas.q: Write the pascal and the joule in SI base units.
Convert 72 km/h to m/s.

children.topic: Q3 · Is F = mv²/r dimensionally a force?
children.note: [mv²/r] = M·L²T⁻²/L = MLT⁻², the same as [ma]. Yes.

manas.q: Show that mv²/r has the dimensions of force.

children.note: 4.7 × 10⁻⁶ m = 4.7 µm. Why: the decimal point moves 6 places to reach 4.7, and 10⁻⁶ is the prefix micro (µ). Check: 4.7 µm × 10⁻⁶ gives back 0.000 004 7 m; that is a bit smaller than a red blood cell.

manas.q: Express 0.0000047 m with a metric prefix.

children.topic: Q5 · A tape reads 3.21 m ± 0.01 m. Percent uncertainty?
children.note: 0.01 / 3.21 × 100 % ≈ 0.3 %. Why: percent uncertainty is the ± amount divided by the reading, so it shows how good the measurement is whatever its size. Check: 0.3 % of 3.21 m is about 0.01 m, the ± we started with.

manas.q: A tape reads 3.21 m ± 0.01 m. What is the percent uncertainty?

children.note: Measure in SI, carry the units through every line, check dimensions before trusting a formula, and report only the digits you know. These four habits catch most engineering errors before they leave the desk.
Next map in this library: Statics — forces, free-body diagrams and equilibrium, where these units (N, N·m) go to work. Medicine and Soil Life libraries use the same SI prefixes.

nodeData.note: Forces, displacements and velocities have a size and a direction. Split them into parts, add them, multiply them — the maths behind statics and dynamics. Own-words notes from OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1 ch. 2 and Wikipedia; examples recomputed. Search words: vector, scalar, components, resultant, SOH CAH TOA, sine rule, cosine rule, dot product, cross product, unit vector, radian.

children.note: A scalar is just a size with a unit: 20 kg, 30 °C, 5 s. A vector also needs a direction: 20 N downward, 3 km east. If turning the arrow changes the answer, the quantity is a vector.

manas.q: What is the difference between a scalar and a vector?

children.note: Mass, time, temperature, energy, speed, distance. Adding them is ordinary arithmetic: 2 kg of sugar plus 3 kg is 5 kg.
Displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, torque, momentum. Two 3 N forces can add to anything from 0 N (opposite) to 6 N (same way).

manas.q: Two forces of 3 N act on a box. What range of totals is possible?

children.note: A matatu that goes from Kencom to Westlands and back has covered a distance but has zero displacement: displacement only cares where you ended up relative to where you started.

manas.q: A matatu drives a loop and returns to the stage. Its displacement?

children.note: Speed is how fast; velocity is how fast and which way. A car going round a roundabout at a steady 30 km/h has constant speed but changing velocity — so it is accelerating.
Bold letter (A), an arrow on top, or underlined in handwriting. The size alone (magnitude) is written A or |A|, always zero or positive.
Right-angled triangles turn a slanted vector into a horizontal part and a vertical part. Three ratios do almost all the work.
sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent. "Opposite" and "adjacent" are named from the angle you are using.

manas.q: State SOH CAH TOA.

children.note: In a right-angled triangle, hypotenuse² = side² + side². A 3 km east and 4 km north trip ends 5 km from the start.
sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹ give the angle back from a ratio. Why it matters: you usually know the components and want the direction.
A full turn is 360° or 2π rad, so 180° = π rad and 1 rad ≈ 57.3°. A radian is the angle where the arc length equals the radius. Rotation formulas (v = ωr) need radians.

manas.q: How many degrees in one radian?

children.note: Before any exam, type sin 30. If you get 0.5 you are in degrees; −0.988 means radians. Many lost marks come from the wrong mode, not wrong physics.

manas.q: Quick test that your calculator is in degree mode?

children.note: A road that rises 1 m for every 10 m along the level (10 % grade) is at tan⁻¹(0.1) = 5.7°. Small angles: the percent grade ÷ 100 is close to the angle in radians.

manas.q: What angle is a 10 % road gradient?

children.note: Any vector in a plane equals an x-part plus a y-part at right angles. Working in components turns hard geometry into two easy sums.

manas.q: Why do engineers split vectors into components?

children.note: For a vector of size A at angle θ above the +x axis: Aₓ = A cos θ, A_y = A sin θ. Check: Aₓ² + A_y² must give back A².

manas.q: Write the x- and y-components of a vector A at angle θ.

children.note: A rope pulls a cart with 500 N at 30° above the ground. Along the ground: 500 cos 30° = 433 N. Lifting part: 500 sin 30° = 250 N. Only the 433 N moves the cart forward.

manas.q: 500 N at 30° above horizontal: horizontal and vertical parts?

children.note: The 250 N upward part reduces how hard the cart presses on the ground, so it also reduces friction. Pulling a little upward can make a heavy load easier to drag.
Arrows of length 1 along x, y and z. A vector is written A = Aₓ i + A_y j (+ A_z k). The numbers in front are the scalar components and can be negative.
If a vector starts at (x₁, y₁) and ends at (x₂, y₂), its components are x₂ − x₁ and y₂ − y₁: end minus start, never the other way.

manas.q: A vector runs from (6, 1.6) to (2, 4.5). Its components?

children.topic: Back from components: size and angle
children.note: Size A = √(Aₓ² + A_y²). Direction tan θ = A_y ÷ Aₓ, measured anticlockwise from +x.
tan⁻¹ only returns −90° to +90°. For a vector with a negative x-part, add 180°. Example: (−4.0, 2.9) gives tan⁻¹ = −35.9°, but the true direction is 144.1°.

manas.q: Vector (−4.0, 2.9): the calculator says −35.9°. True direction?

children.note: Sketch it first. A vector pointing left and up must be between 90° and 180°; if the answer is not there, fix the quadrant.
Size and angle (A, θ) are polar coordinates; (Aₓ, A_y) are Cartesian. Same vector, two descriptions — convert with cos/sin one way and Pythagoras/tan the other.
The total of several vectors is called the resultant. Add by drawing (tip to tail) or, more accurately, by adding components.

manas.q: What is a resultant?

children.note: Draw the first arrow, start the second at its tip, and so on. The resultant runs from the first tail to the last tip. The order does not change the answer.
Put two vectors tail to tail and complete the parallelogram; the diagonal from the shared tail is their sum. Same answer as tip to tail.
Add all the x-parts, add all the y-parts, then rebuild size and angle. Works for any number of vectors and needs no scale drawing.

manas.q: Describe the component method for adding vectors.

children.topic: Worked: two forces on a hook

manas.q: 300 N at 0° plus 400 N at 60°: size and direction of the resultant?

children.note: The triangle formed has the angle 120° between the two sides: R² = 300² + 400² − 2·300·400·cos 120° = 370 000, so R = 608 N. Two methods agree.
sin φ ÷ 400 = sin 120° ÷ 608 gives φ = 34.7°, the same angle from +x.
A matatu goes 3.0 km east then 4.0 km north. Displacement: √(3² + 4²) = 5.0 km at tan⁻¹(4/3) = 53° north of east. The road distance is 7.0 km.

manas.q: 3.0 km east then 4.0 km north: displacement?

children.note: Fuel and fares depend on distance (7 km); a drone flying straight only needs the displacement (5 km).
A − B means A + (−B): flip B round and add it. Used for change in velocity, Δv = v_final − v_initial.
3A is three times as long, same direction. −A is the same length pointing the opposite way. Dividing a vector by its own size gives the unit vector of its direction.
For A = 3i + 4j, size 5, the unit vector is 0.6i + 0.8j. Multiply it by any size to get a vector that way.

manas.q: Unit vector in the direction of 3i + 4j?

children.note: For triangles without a right angle — truss members, cable pairs, survey lines.
c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C, where C is the angle opposite side c. When C = 90° it becomes Pythagoras. Use it when you know two sides and the angle between them.

manas.q: State the cosine rule. When does it reduce to Pythagoras?

children.note: a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B = c ÷ sin C. Use it when you know a side and the angle opposite it, plus one more piece.

manas.q: State the sine rule.

children.note: Given two sides and a non-included angle, the sine rule can give two possible triangles (sin x = sin(180° − x)). Sketch to decide which one is real.
If the angle between two force arrows (tail to tail) is θ, the triangle angle opposite the resultant is 180° − θ. So R² = a² + b² + 2ab cos θ. Mixing these two angles is a common error.

manas.q: Two forces with angle θ between them: resultant squared by cosine rule?

children.note: A · B = AB cos φ, where φ is the angle between them. The result is a scalar. It measures how much one vector points along the other.

manas.q: What is the dot product and is its result a scalar or a vector?

children.note: A · B = AₓBₓ + A_yB_y + A_zB_z. Because i · i = 1 and i · j = 0.

children.topic: Finding the angle between two vectors

manas.q: Angle between (3, 4) and (4, 3)?

children.note: If A · B = 0 (and neither is zero), they are at 90°. Quick check that a normal force is really perpendicular to a slope.

manas.q: What does a zero dot product tell you?

children.topic: Use: work done by a force
children.note: Work = F · d. A 50 N pull at 60° to the ground over 10 m does 50 × 10 × cos 60° = 250 J — only the part of the force along the motion counts.

manas.q: 50 N at 60° to the motion, 10 m: work done?

children.topic: Why a carried bag does no work horizontally
children.note: Your upward hold is at 90° to the walk, so cos 90° = 0. You get tired from muscles, but the force does no work on the bag along the road.
The part of A along a direction with unit vector u is A · u. Example: weight along a slope.
A × B is a vector at right angles to both, of size AB sin φ. It gives torque and the force on a current in a magnetic field.

manas.q: What is the size and direction of A × B?

children.note: Point the fingers of your right hand along A, curl them toward B; the thumb points along A × B. Order matters: B × A is the opposite direction.

manas.q: Is A × B equal to B × A?

children.note: i × j = k, j × k = i, k × i = j (go round in order); reversing the order gives a minus sign. Any vector crossed with itself is zero.
τ = r × F, size rF sin φ. 80 N at the end of a 0.25 m spanner, at right angles: 20 N·m. At 60° to the handle: 20 × sin 60° = 17.3 N·m.

manas.q: 80 N on a 0.25 m spanner at 60° to the handle: torque?

children.note: sin φ is largest (1) at 90°. Pushing along the handle (φ = 0) turns nothing — the same lever-arm idea as the statics map.
AB sin φ is the area of the parallelogram the two vectors make. Used later for areas and flux.
Choose axes along and across the slope — the motion is along it, so one component equation becomes simple.

children.topic: Weight on a slope at angle θ
children.note: Along the slope: mg sin θ (pulls it down the slope). Into the slope: mg cos θ (pressed into the surface, balanced by the normal force).

manas.q: Weight components along and into a slope at θ?

children.topic: Worked: loaded matatu on a 10 % grade
children.note: Mass 1500 kg, weight 14 700 N, angle 5.7°. Down-slope part: 14 700 × sin 5.7° ≈ 1460 N. The engine must supply this extra force just to hold speed uphill.

manas.q: 1500 kg vehicle on a 10 % grade: weight component down the slope?

children.note: sin θ ≈ 0.1 for a 10 % grade, so about one tenth of the weight: 1470 N. Close to the exact answer.
The angle between the weight and the "into the slope" axis equals the slope angle θ. Draw a steep slope to test: as θ → 90°, the down-slope part should become the whole weight (sin 90° = 1).
These cost marks in first-year tests.
3 N + 4 N is 7 N only if they point the same way; at right angles it is 5 N. Always add components.
Cos goes with the side next to the angle you use. If the angle is measured from the vertical, the horizontal part uses sin.

manas.q: A force makes angle α with the vertical. Horizontal part?

children.note: tan⁻¹ only answers between −90° and +90°. For (−3, 4) it says −53.1°, but that vector points left and up, so the real angle is −53.1° + 180° = 126.9°. Check the signs of the components and sketch; add 180° when x is negative.

sin 30 should be 0.5. In radian mode the calculator gives −0.988, because 30 rad is almost five full turns. Quick check before any test: work out sin 30 — if it is not 0.5, set degree (DEG) mode, or convert with × π/180.
A component pointing left or down is negative. Lose the sign and a force that should cancel will double instead.
Dot gives a number (work, projection); cross gives a vector (torque). Dot uses cos, cross uses sin.

manas.q: Which product gives torque, and which gives work?

children.note: Say the answer aloud; tap a bubble for the source page.

children.topic: Q1 · 200 N at 40° above horizontal: parts?

manas.q: 200 N at 40° above horizontal: horizontal and vertical parts?
Add (2i + 5j) N and (4i − 3j) N. Size?

children.note: Dot product (2)(1) + (−1)(2) = 2 − 2 = 0, so yes. Why: A · B = AB cos φ and cos 90° = 0, so a zero dot product means a right angle. Check by sketch: (2, −1) points right and down, (1, 2) up and right — a quarter turn apart.

manas.q: Are (2, −1) and (1, 2) perpendicular?

children.note: π/2 ≈ 1.571 rad and π/4 ≈ 0.785 rad. Multiply degrees by π/180.

manas.q: Convert 45° to radians.

children.topic: Q5 · Two 100 N forces 120° apart: resultant?
children.note: R² = 100² + 100² + 2·100·100·cos 120° = 10 000, so R = 100 N, pointing midway between them.

manas.q: Two 100 N forces 120° apart: resultant size?

children.note: Sketch, choose axes, split every vector into components with sin and cos, add the x-parts and the y-parts, then rebuild the size and angle — checking the quadrant. Dot gives "how much along"; cross gives "how much turning".
Earlier maps: Units, dimensions and estimation; Statics (ΣF = 0 is a vector sum; torque is a cross product). Next: Dynamics — Newton's second law uses the same components.

maps.title: Statics: forces, free-body diagrams and equilibrium

nodeData.topic: Statics: forces, free-body diagrams and equilibrium
nodeData.note: Why a bridge, a roof truss or a water-tank stand stays still: the forces and the turning effects on it add to zero. Own-words notes from OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1 (free, CC BY) sections 5.7, 12.1, 12.2; tap a bubble for the page. SI units, g = 9.8 m/s². Search words: statics, equilibrium, free body diagram, FBD, torque, moment, lever arm, reaction, tension, normal force, friction.

children.note: Equilibrium for a rigid body: zero linear acceleration and zero angular (turning) acceleration at the same time. At rest in our frame it is in static equilibrium; moving at constant velocity it is in dynamic equilibrium — the same equations apply.

manas.q: Define equilibrium of a rigid body.

children.note: A particle has no size, so only forces matter. A rigid body has size, so where a force acts matters too — that is what adds torque to the problem.
A crate at rest on a moving lorry is in static equilibrium for the driver and dynamic equilibrium for someone on the road. The laws are the same in every inertial frame.

children.topic: Newton's first law is the statics law
children.note: No net force → no change in motion. Statics is Newton's first law applied to forces and to torques.

manas.q: Which of Newton's laws does statics rest on?

children.note: Six forces cover most first-year problems. Each has a fixed direction rule — learn the rule and the diagram draws itself.

manas.q: List the common forces and the direction each one acts in.

children.note: Acts at the centre of mass. A 20 kg beam weighs 20 × 9.8 = 196 N. The only common force that needs no contact.

manas.q: What is the weight of a 60 kg person on Earth?

children.topic: Normal force N, perpendicular to the surface
children.note: The push of a surface on the body, always at right angles to the surface and away from it. On a slope it is tilted, not vertical.

children.topic: Tension T, along the rope, away from the body
children.note: A rope can only pull. The same tension acts at both ends of a light rope.

children.topic: Friction f, along the surface, opposing motion
children.note: Opposes the motion or the intended motion. Static friction can be anything up to a maximum μₛN; kinetic friction is μₖN.

manas.q: In which direction does friction act on a block held still on a slope?

children.note: A hand, a cable from a winch, a wind load — drawn at the angle the problem states.

children.topic: Spring force, towards the natural length
children.note: Proportional to the stretch or compression (Hooke's law). Pushes or pulls back towards the unstretched position.
What a support can push back with depends on how it is made. Count the unknowns a support brings before you count equations.

manas.q: How many unknowns do a roller, a pin and a fixed support each add?

children.note: One force perpendicular to the surface. It cannot pull or resist sliding.
A force of unknown size and direction — write it as two components. It cannot resist turning.
Two force components plus a moment, because the wall stops the beam turning. A cantilever balcony is this case.
Draw the body alone, with every external force on it as an arrow. Done right, the diagram is most of the solution; done wrong, no algebra can save it.

manas.q: State the four rules for a free-body diagram.

children.note: Sketch the object (a dot if treating it as a particle) with x–y axes. Circle it so you only mark forces acting ON it.

children.topic: Rule 2: all external forces, no net force
children.note: Weight, normal, tension, friction, applied, spring. Never draw the net force; never draw forces the body exerts on other things; never both halves of an action–reaction pair.

manas.q: Name two things that must never appear on a free-body diagram.

children.topic: Rule 3: replace angled forces by components
children.note: Draw the x and y components and put a squiggle through the original arrow so you do not count it twice.
Two blocks, two diagrams. Forces between them appear on both, equal and opposite.
If the body accelerates, note the acceleration beside the diagram in another colour, not as an arrow on it.
Forces: pull P at 30° above the ground, weight down, normal up, friction backwards. Components of P: P cos 30° forward, P sin 30° upward — the upward part reduces the normal force.

manas.q: A sled is pulled by 100 N at 30°. Forward and upward components?

children.note: Forward 100 × cos 30° = 86.6 N; upward 100 × sin 30° = 50 N. Check: 86.6² + 50² ≈ 100².

children.topic: Example: two blocks on an incline
children.note: Block A on top of block B on a slope: separate diagrams. Friction from B on A points one way; friction from A on B the opposite way — they are a third-law pair, equal in size.
Ask: which way would the body slide if the surface were ice? Friction points the other way.

children.topic: First condition: forces sum to zero
children.note: ΣF = 0, which in components means ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0 (and ΣFz = 0 in 3-D). This alone solves particle problems — knots, hanging loads, blocks held on slopes.

manas.q: Write the first equilibrium condition in component form.

children.topic: Worked: lamp on two symmetric cables
children.note: A 5.0 kg lamp (49 N) hangs from two cables, each 30° above horizontal. Vertical: 2T sin 30° = 49, so T = 49 N. Horizontal: the two T cos 30° cancel by symmetry.

manas.q: A 5 kg lamp hangs from two cables at 30° above horizontal. Tension in each?

children.note: At 10° above horizontal: T = 49 / (2 sin 10°) = 141 N — nearly three times the lamp's weight. A perfectly horizontal cable would need infinite tension, which is why washing lines sag.

manas.q: Why can a clothes line never be pulled perfectly straight?

children.topic: Worked: block held on a 30° slope
children.note: 10 kg block at rest on a 30° incline. Along the slope: friction f = mg sin 30° = 98 × 0.5 = 49 N, up the slope. Perpendicular: N = mg cos 30° = 84.9 N.

manas.q: A 10 kg block rests on a 30° slope: find the friction and normal force.

children.note: μ must be at least f/N = 49/84.9 = 0.58 = tan 30°. In general a block stays put while tan θ ≤ μₛ.

children.topic: Choose axes to suit the problem
children.note: On a slope, take x along the slope and y perpendicular to it; then N has no x-component and only weight needs splitting.
Στ = 0: the turning effects about any axis also cancel. Needed whenever the body has size — beams, ladders, seesaws, cranes, bridge decks.

manas.q: Write the second equilibrium condition and say when it is needed.

children.note: τ = r F sin θ: the force times the perpendicular distance from the pivot to its line of action. Unit N·m (not joules, though the base units match).

manas.q: A 200 N force acts 1.5 m from a hinge at right angles. Torque?

children.note: Pick one sense as positive and keep it. Many textbooks and this library use anticlockwise = +.

children.topic: A force through the pivot has zero torque
children.note: Its lever arm is zero. This is the trick for choosing the pivot: put it where an unknown force acts, and that unknown disappears from the torque equation.

manas.q: Where should you put the pivot to make an unknown force vanish from the torque equation?

children.note: If forces sum to zero and torques about one point sum to zero, then torques about every other point sum to zero too — shifting the pivot adds R × ΣF, which is zero. So you choose the pivot for convenience.

manas.q: Why are we free to choose any pivot point in an equilibrium problem?

children.note: With the z-axis as the rotation axis the six equations shrink to ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, Στz = 0. Three unknowns at most can be found; more unknowns means the problem is statically indeterminate.

manas.q: How many independent equilibrium equations does a planar problem give?

children.topic: Centre of mass carries the weight
children.note: For torque purposes, a uniform beam's whole weight acts at its midpoint; a uniform plate's at its centre.
Find the centre of mass first (given, or by balancing). A loaded lorry or a crane with its boom out has it well away from the geometric middle.
OpenStax's problem-solving strategy for rigid bodies in equilibrium. Follow it in order every time; most mistakes come from skipping step 2.

manas.q: List the five steps for solving a static-equilibrium problem.

children.topic: 1 · Identify the body, the forces, the question
children.note: Which object? What acts on it? What is asked, and what is given — including facts hidden in the wording ("uniform beam" means weight at the centre).

children.topic: 2 · Draw the free-body diagram and pick a pivot
children.note: Axes, every force, components, labels. For an unknown force guess a direction; a negative answer later means it points the other way. Mark the pivot and the lever arms.

manas.q: What does a negative answer for an unknown force mean?

children.note: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, Στ = 0 about the chosen pivot, each force with its sign.
As many equations as unknowns. Keep symbols until the end; substitute numbers last.
Right unit (N or N·m)? Sensible size? Re-solve about a different pivot as an independent check.
Three problems, each recomputed step by step. Cover the answer and try first.

children.topic: A · Seesaw: where must the heavier child sit?
children.note: A 30 kg child sits 2.0 m left of the pivot. A 40 kg child sits on the right at distance d. Torques about the pivot: 30 × 9.8 × 2.0 = 40 × 9.8 × d, so d = 60/40 = 1.5 m. (g cancels.)

manas.q: 30 kg at 2.0 m balances 40 kg at what distance?

children.note: ΣFy = 0: the pivot pushes up with (30 + 40) × 9.8 = 686 N.

children.topic: B · Beam on two supports with a load
children.note: Uniform beam, 4.0 m, 20 kg (196 N at its middle, 2.0 m from A). A 60 kg load (588 N) sits 1.0 m from support A. Find the support reactions R_A and R_B.

manas.q: Set up the torque equation about A for the beam example.

children.note: R_B × 4.0 = 196 × 2.0 + 588 × 1.0 = 392 + 588 = 980 N·m, so R_B = 245 N. R_A drops out because it acts at A.
R_A + R_B = 196 + 588 = 784 N, so R_A = 784 − 245 = 539 N. The support nearer the load carries more — as expected.

manas.q: In the beam example, why does R_A carry more than R_B?

children.note: R_A × 4.0 = 196 × 2.0 + 588 × 3.0 = 392 + 1764 = 2156 N·m, so R_A = 539 N. Same answer from a different pivot: solved.
A 1000 L tank (1000 kg of water, 9800 N) plus a 200 kg tank-and-frame (1960 N) stands on four equal legs. Symmetry: each leg carries 11 760 / 4 = 2940 N. Each leg's footing must take about 3 kN.

manas.q: A full 1000 L tank on a 200 kg stand with four legs: load per leg?

children.note: Symmetry breaks; use torques about one pair of legs to find how the load shifts — the legs under the heavy side carry more. This is why stands are levelled.
Each of these has been seen in first-year scripts — and in collapsed sheds.

children.topic: Drawing the net force or "ma" as a force
children.note: Only real pushes and pulls from other bodies go on the diagram: weight, normal, tension, friction. Why: ma is the result of those forces, not one more force — drawing it counts it twice. Check: name the body behind every arrow.

children.topic: Normal force drawn vertical on a slope
children.note: It is perpendicular to the surface, so it tilts with the slope. Why: the surface can only push straight out of itself. Example: a 10 kg box on a 30° ramp has N = mg cos 30° = 98 × 0.866 ≈ 85 N, not 98 N. Check: at 0° (flat) cos 0° = 1 and N = mg again.

children.topic: Both halves of an action–reaction pair on one body
children.note: They act on different bodies; only one belongs on any single diagram. Why: put both on one body and they cancel, so nothing could ever be pushed. Example: a book on a table — the table pushes up on the book (book's diagram); the book pushes down on the table (table's diagram).

children.topic: Using the full distance instead of the lever arm
children.note: Torque needs the perpendicular distance, or r F sin θ. A force along the line to the pivot turns nothing.

Decide the positive sense once; write every torque with that sign. Why: one flipped sign turns a balance into a sum and gives a reaction that is too big or negative. Example: in the 4 m beam, anticlockwise positive about A: R_B × 4.0 − 196 × 2.0 − 588 × 1.0 = 0 → R_B = 245 N. Check: a negative reaction means a sign slipped (or the support must pull down).
Three unknowns per planar body. A fourth needs another body's diagram or a deformation argument (second year).
"Uniform beam of 20 kg" is a force at the midpoint — it is part of the problem.
Say the answer aloud; tap a bubble for the source page.

ΣF = 0 (no push left over, so it does not slide off) and Στ = 0 about any axis (no turn left over, so it does not spin). Why both: a ladder can have ΣF = 0 and still tip over if the torques do not cancel.

manas.q: State the two conditions for static equilibrium.

children.topic: Q2 · 80 kg person on a 2.0 m plank, 0.5 m from end A
children.note: Weight 784 N. About A: R_B × 2.0 = 784 × 0.5 → R_B = 196 N; R_A = 588 N (plank weight ignored).

manas.q: An 80 kg person stands 0.5 m from end A of a light 2.0 m plank. Reactions?

children.topic: Q3 · Why put the pivot at a hinge?
children.note: The unknown hinge force passes through the pivot and has zero torque, leaving one equation with one unknown.

manas.q: Why choose the hinge as the pivot?

children.topic: Q4 · Cable at 20° holding a 300 N sign, two cables
children.note: Only the upward parts hold the sign: 2T sin 20° = 300, so T = 300 / (2 × 0.342) = 439 N each. Why so big: a flat cable has a small upward part, so it must pull hard. Check: hanging straight down (90°) each would carry just 150 N.

manas.q: Two cables at 20° above horizontal hold a 300 N sign. Tension in each?

children.topic: Q5 · Is a car cruising at constant 80 km/h in equilibrium?
children.note: Yes — dynamic equilibrium: no acceleration, forces and torques balance.

manas.q: Is a car at a steady 80 km/h on a straight road in equilibrium?

children.note: Isolate the body, draw every real force, write ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0 about a pivot that kills an unknown, solve, then check with another pivot. The free-body diagram is the whole skill; the algebra is routine.
Previous map: Units, dimensions and estimation (N and N·m). Coming next in this library: Dynamics (Newton's second law), Materials (stress and strain — what the 3 kN per leg does to the steel).

nodeData.topic: Dynamics: Newton's second law, worked problems
nodeData.note: Statics asks why things stay still; dynamics asks how they speed up and slow down. ΣF = ma plus a free-body diagram solves most first-year problems. Own-words notes from OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1 ch. 5–6 and Wikipedia; examples recomputed with g = 9.8 m/s². Search words: Newton, F = ma, net force, mass, weight, friction, tension, lift, elevator, Atwood, braking distance, third law, dynamics.

children.topic: The three laws in one line each
children.note: Newton's laws link forces to motion. First: no net force, no change in motion. Second: net force = mass × acceleration. Third: forces come in equal and opposite pairs on two different bodies.

manas.q: State Newton's three laws in one line each.

children.note: A body keeps its velocity (including zero) unless a net force acts. A passenger lurches forward when a matatu brakes because their body carries on at the old speed.

manas.q: Why do standing passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes?

children.note: ΣF = ma: add every force on the body as vectors to get the net force; the acceleration points the same way as that net force.
If A pushes B, B pushes A equally and oppositely. The two forces act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other on one diagram.
The laws hold in frames that are not accelerating (inertial frames). Inside a braking bus, the "forward push" you feel is not a real force — it is the bus slowing under you.
The law is a vector equation, so write it once for each axis: ΣFₓ = maₓ and ΣF_y = ma_y.

manas.q: Write Newton's second law in component form.

children.note: Only the sum of all forces decides acceleration. A car at a steady 80 km/h has a big engine force but zero net force, because drag and rolling resistance balance it.

manas.q: A car cruises at a steady speed. What is the net force on it?

children.note: 1 N is the force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s²: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s². A 100 g apple weighs about 1 N.

manas.q: Define one newton in base units.

children.note: Same force, double the mass, half the acceleration. Mass is measured in kg and does not change from place to place.
The general law is ΣF = rate of change of momentum (p = mv). For a fixed mass this becomes ma. The momentum form handles rockets and conveyor belts that gain or lose mass.
A 2000 kg loaded matatu goes from 0 to 50 km/h (13.9 m/s) in 10 s. a = 13.9 ÷ 10 = 1.39 m/s². Net force = 2000 × 1.39 ≈ 2780 N.

manas.q: 2000 kg, 0 to 50 km/h in 10 s: acceleration and net force?

children.note: 2780 N is the net force. The tyres must push forward by 2780 N plus whatever drag and rolling resistance oppose the motion.
Mass is how much matter (kg). Weight is the gravitational pull on it (N): w = mg, with g = 9.8 m/s² near the Earth's surface.

manas.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?

children.note: Weight = 70 × 9.8 = 686 N. Bathroom scales show 70 "kg" because they divide the force by g.

manas.q: Weight of a 70 kg person?

children.note: Problems use g = 9.8 m/s². The real value differs a little from place to place on Earth — too little to matter in first-year work. Weight changes with g; mass does not.
Shops say "kilograms" for weight; engineers keep kg for mass and N for force. Writing "a force of 50 kg" in a script loses marks.
Almost every problem uses a few named forces. Each has a rule for its direction.
Always straight down toward the Earth's centre, acting at the centre of mass.
A surface pushes back at right angles to itself. It is not always equal to mg — it changes on slopes and in lifts.

manas.q: Is the normal force always equal to mg?

children.note: A rope or cable can only pull, along its own length. A light rope over a smooth pulley has the same tension on both sides.
Acts along the surface, opposing sliding (or the tendency to slide). Static up to μₛN; kinetic about μₖN.
Proportional to stretch or squeeze and opposite to it: F = −kx (Hooke's law), k in N/m.

manas.q: What is Hooke's law?

children.note: Air or water resistance, growing with speed. At highway speeds it is the main force the engine fights.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

children.note: Five steps; the free-body diagram is where the marks are won.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

manas.q: List the five steps for solving a Newton's-law problem.

children.note: Choose which object you will analyse. Choosing well can remove forces you do not know.
Every external force as an arrow from the body. Never draw "ma" as a force.
One axis along the acceleration if you know its direction (along a slope, up a lift shaft).

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

children.topic: 4 · Write ΣF = ma for each axis
children.note: Signs: forces along the positive axis are +, the others −. If the body does not accelerate on an axis, that sum is zero.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

children.note: Units in N, m/s², kg. Test extreme cases: if friction were zero, or the angle 90°, does the answer behave sensibly?

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

children.note: A 60 kg person stands on a scale in a lift. The scale reads the normal force N. Up is positive: N − mg = ma.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

manas.q: What does a bathroom scale actually measure?

children.note: N = m(g + a) = 60 × 11.0 = 660 N. The scale shows 660 ÷ 9.8 = 67.3 "kg" — you feel heavier.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

manas.q: 60 kg person, lift accelerating up at 1.2 m/s²: scale reading in N?

children.note: a = 0, so N = mg = 588 N; the scale shows 60 "kg". Speed alone does not change the reading.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

manas.q: Lift moving up at constant speed: does the scale read more?

children.note: N = m(g − a) = 60 × 8.6 = 516 N, shown as 52.7 "kg" — you feel lighter.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

children.note: An 800 kg car accelerating up at 1.0 m/s² needs T = 800 × (9.8 + 1.0) = 8640 N. Real lifts add a large safety factor; check the current standard before any design.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

children.note: Bodies tied together share one acceleration. Solve the whole system first for a, then one body for the tension.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

manas.q: How do you find the tension between two connected blocks?

children.topic: Two blocks pulled on a smooth table
children.note: 4 kg and 6 kg joined by a string; 20 N pulls the 6 kg block. Whole system: a = 20 ÷ 10 = 2.0 m/s². The string is the only force on the 4 kg block: T = 4 × 2.0 = 8.0 N.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

manas.q: 4 kg and 6 kg tied together, 20 N pull on the 6 kg: acceleration and string tension?

children.note: On the 6 kg block: 20 − T = 6 × 2.0 = 12, so T = 8.0 N. Same answer.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

children.note: 5 kg and 3 kg hang over a smooth pulley. a = (5 − 3) ÷ (5 + 3) × 9.8 = 2.45 m/s². Tension T = 2 × 5 × 3 × 9.8 ÷ 8 = 36.8 N.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

manas.q: Atwood machine with 5 kg and 3 kg: acceleration?

children.note: T lies between the two weights (29.4 N and 49 N). If the masses were equal, a = 0 and T = mg.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

children.note: A 1200 kg car is towed with a = 0.50 m/s² against 300 N of rolling resistance. Rope tension = 1200 × 0.50 + 300 = 900 N.

links.label: 📘 OpenStax 6.1 Solving problems with Newton's laws

manas.q: Towing 1200 kg at 0.50 m/s² against 300 N resistance: rope tension?

children.note: Static friction holds things still up to a limit; once sliding, kinetic friction is usually smaller. That is why a stuck box suddenly "breaks free".

manas.q: Why is it harder to start a box sliding than to keep it sliding?

children.note: Approximate values: rubber on dry concrete μₛ 1.0, μₖ 0.7; on wet concrete μₖ 0.3–0.5; wood on wood 0.5 / 0.3; steel on steel (dry) 0.6 / 0.3. Real values vary with surface and wear.
Wood on wood: N = 490 N. To start: 0.5 × 490 = 245 N. To keep sliding: 0.3 × 490 = 147 N. A 200 N push does not move it (friction matches 200 N).

manas.q: 50 kg crate, μₛ = 0.5, μₖ = 0.3: force to start it moving?

children.note: Once sliding, only kinetic friction (147 N) pushes back. a = (300 − 147) ÷ 50 = 3.06 m/s². Why: only the net force speeds the crate up — the 147 N lost to friction turns into heat, not speed. Check: the same 300 N on ice (almost no friction) would give 300 ÷ 50 = 6 m/s².
Block on a 30° slope with μₖ = 0.3: a = g(sin 30° − 0.3 cos 30°) = 2.35 m/s². Mass cancels — heavy and light blocks slide alike.

manas.q: Block sliding down 30° with μₖ = 0.3: acceleration?

children.note: A crate rides on a lorry only by static friction. The most the lorry can accelerate without it sliding is μₛg; with μₛ = 0.5 that is 4.9 m/s². Why loads must be strapped.

manas.q: Crate on a lorry bed, μₛ = 0.5: maximum acceleration before it slides?

children.note: Car at 72 km/h (20 m/s), locked wheels, rubber on dry concrete μₖ 0.7: a = 6.86 m/s², distance = v² ÷ 2a = 29 m. On wet road with μₖ 0.4: 51 m.

manas.q: 20 m/s, μₖ = 0.7: braking distance after the wheels lock?

children.note: Reaction time (about a second at 20 m/s adds 20 m), ABS keeping tyres at static grip, worn tyres and slopes. A road-safety figure, not a design value.
Distance grows with v². Twice the speed, four times the braking distance.

manas.q: If speed doubles, what happens to braking distance?

children.note: Every force has a partner on another body. Finding the partner tells you which body to draw.
Your foot pushes the ground backward; the ground pushes you forward (friction). Tyres do the same — on mud, the push fails and the wheels spin.

manas.q: What force pushes a car forward?

children.note: "If the cart pulls back on the donkey equally, how can they move?" Because the two forces act on different bodies. The donkey moves forward because the ground pushes it harder than the cart pulls back.

children.topic: Weight and normal force are NOT a pair
children.note: Both act on the same body. The partner of your weight is your pull on the Earth; the partner of the normal force is your push on the floor.

children.note: ma is the result of the forces, not one of them. Why: F = ma says the forces add up to ma; drawing ma as an extra arrow counts the same effect twice. Example: a 2 kg trolley pulled with 10 N on smooth ground has one horizontal arrow (10 N) and a = 5 m/s²; add an "ma" arrow and the sum becomes 20 N, which is wrong.

Only true on level ground with no vertical acceleration and no slanted pull. Work it out from ΣF_y each time. Example: pull a 10 kg box with 50 N at 30° above level. The pull lifts it by 50 × sin 30° = 25 N, so N = 98 − 25 = 73 N, not 98 N — and the friction gets smaller with it.

Force in N. Multiply by g to turn mass into weight. Why: kg measures how much matter there is; N measures a push or pull. Example: a 50 kg sack weighs 50 × 9.8 = 490 N, not "50" — put 50 into ΣF = ma as a force and every answer is about 10 times too small.

children.topic: Forgetting friction can be less than μₛN
children.note: μₛN is the maximum. A box that is not moving has exactly as much friction as needed to balance the push.

manas.q: Is static friction always equal to μₛN?

children.note: They act on different bodies and never appear on the same diagram.

Divide km/h by 3.6 before using F = ma or the motion equations. Why: the equations assume metres and seconds, and 1 km/h is only 1/3.6 m/s. Example: a car braking from 54 km/h in 5 s: 54 ÷ 3.6 = 15 m/s, so a = 3 m/s²; using 54 directly gives 10.8 m/s², more than g — a sign something is wrong.
